passage:
Somewhere between one and four in the afternoon, most people become noticeably less alert. Reaction times slow, mistakes increase, and drivers are more likely to crash. The dip happens whether or not lunch was eaten, which rules out the usual explanation about a heavy meal.

Sleep researchers regard it as built in. The body's internal clock produces two low points in each twenty-four hours: a deep one in the small hours and a shallower one in the early afternoon. Cultures that developed in hot climates arranged the working day around the second, closing shops in the middle of the day and reopening in the cooler evening.

Laboratory work supports the practice. A nap of ten to twenty minutes improves alertness for two to three hours afterwards, and does so more reliably than caffeine. Longer naps are risky: sleeping beyond about thirty minutes brings the sleeper into deeper stages, and waking from those produces a heavy, confused feeling that can last half an hour and leaves the person worse off than before.

Several large companies have installed rooms for the purpose, and some hospitals now schedule naps for staff on night shifts, having found that the alternative is errors. Where they exist, take-up is high.

The obstacle is not evidence but appearance. In many workplaces sleeping is read as a sign that somebody is not committed, and the employee who takes a twenty-minute nap looks lazier than the one who stares at a screen for three unproductive hours. Changing that impression has proved considerably harder than finding somewhere to lie down.
